abstract: Long-term observations are essential to resolve how ecosystems respond to environmental variability, yet decadal-scale molecular time series of marine plankton communities remain rare. Here, we analysed a >20-year (2001-2023) high-frequency 18S rRNA gene (V9) metabarcoding time series of eukaryotic plankton from a coastal observatory in the Western English Channel. Community composition exhibited recurrent seasonal cycles driven primarily by seawater temperature and water column stratification. Superimposed on this seasonal baseline, we identified a pronounced but transient community shift between 2008 and 2011, characterised by reduced diversity, and distinct community structuring, indicating plankton ecosystem-wide biodiversity turnover. This period reflected marked community reorganisation, with potential declines in larger plankton taxa (including copepods and diatoms) and concurrent increases in picoeukaryotes and heterotrophic stramenopiles, consistent with a shift toward smaller-sized, microbial communities. While temperature explained much of the seasonal-scale variation, it did not account for the proposed biodiversity turnover. Instead, the shift was associated with negative phases of the North Atlantic Oscillation, implicating basin-scale climate forcing. Following 2011, communities returned to a state resembling earlier years, indicating a reversible, rather than persistent, change. These findings demonstrate that coastal plankton communities can undergo rapid, climate-driven but reversible biodiversity turnover that is not captured by seasonal dynamics alone and highlight the power of long-term metabarcoding time series to detect transient and recoverable ecologically significant community reorganisation.
